context:
Profiling gene expression in its spatial context is important for understanding how tumors progress and resist therapy. Spatial transcriptomics measures expression across intact tissue, with platforms ranging from targeted panels to transcriptome-wide assays and from near-cellular to multicellular resolution. Sequencing-based capture strategies use positional barcodes to preserve tissue coordinates and can be applied to fresh-frozen or formalin-fixed material. However, a capture location commonly spans tens of micrometres and may contain a mixture of malignant, immune, stromal, and other cells. The number and composition of cells can also vary substantially between tumor regions. Resolving the cellular composition of each location is therefore necessary before the spatial cellular landscape can be interpreted.

Existing deconvolution approaches were largely developed for general spatial transcriptomics or bulk expression profiles and face tumor-specific limitations. Some require suitable malignant reference profiles, which are difficult to define because malignant expression programs vary across patients and tumor types. Approaches that assign unexplained signal to an unknown compartment may not distinguish cancer cells from genuinely unrepresented normal cell types. Methods that force all inferred fractions at every location to sum to the same total can also make estimates difficult to compare when tissue cellularity changes across a section. Paired single-cell sequencing can provide sample-specific references, but it requires fresh material, additional work, and cost, and is often unavailable for archived specimens. Dissociation can also selectively reduce recovery of fragile populations.

The kidneys maintain fluid and electrolyte balance, remove metabolic waste, and contribute to blood-pressure regulation. Acute injury can disrupt these functions within hours or days, while repeated or unresolved injury can promote chronic kidney disease and eventual kidney failure. Renal injury affects both tubular epithelial cells and the surrounding interstitial environment. Damaged tubules may enter stress responses, proliferate, change differentiation state, or attempt to rebuild normal epithelial structure. Some responses restore function, whereas others persist and become maladaptive. Stromal, vascular, and immune populations can support repair or contribute to inflammation and fibrosis. The balance among these processes varies across nephron segments, anatomical regions, injury stages, and individuals.

A central challenge is to define the molecular diversity underlying successful and unsuccessful repair at cellular resolution while preserving tissue context. This requires distinguishing reference identities from injury-associated states, determining whether altered populations are transient or persistent, and understanding how local environments influence recovery. Molecular profiles must also be interpreted in relation to corticomedullary organization because specialized epithelial and interstitial compartments have different physiological roles. Regulatory state, genetic susceptibility, and patient outcomes provide complementary views of whether an apparently adaptive response ultimately protects or harms kidney function.

Pathology decisions are made from complex and sometimes limited evidence. Machine-learning systems trained on modest cohorts may generalize poorly, particularly for uncommon cancers or outcome prediction across institutions. Large collections of histopathology images have enabled pretrained image models that provide reusable representations of tissue morphology. Spatial transcriptomics and related multi-omic assays measure molecular features while preserving their positions in a tissue section. Depending on the assay, these measurements may include RNA, proteins, chromatin accessibility, or other molecular layers. Biological descriptions and prior knowledge provide another potentially relevant modality.

Histopathology and spatial molecular measurements are naturally linked because sequencing locations are registered to a tissue slide. Image morphology may complement expression, while molecular profiles can clarify the biological meaning of visually similar regions. Yet these sources differ in scale, noise, dimensionality, and semantics. Molecular measurements can be sparse; image representations are learned from morphology and may not retain features needed for a molecular or clinical question. Spatial assays produce observations nested within slides, whereas diagnosis, treatment response, prognosis, and reporting are often assigned at the patient or whole-slide level. Joint representations must preserve correspondence among morphology, molecular measurements, language, and location while allowing a fair assessment of what each modality contributes.

Spatially resolved omics technologies provide molecular measurements together with the physical locations of cells or other spatial units in intact tissue. These data can connect tissue microanatomy with function and support clinically relevant tasks such as diagnosis, monitoring disease progression, and patient stratification. Making such connections requires representations that simplify complex spatial measurements while retaining biological information and remaining interpretable to domain experts.

Clustering or phenotyping assigns each measured unit to a cell type, state, or spatial domain, usually from molecular profiles and prior markers. A sample can then be summarized by the abundance and distribution of these labels. Neighborhood analysis goes beyond individual labels by describing which cell types or states co-occur locally. Some approaches test pairwise enrichment in immediate neighborhoods, others cluster local compositions into recurring niches, and graph approaches learn embeddings from spatial adjacency. These strategies have limitations. Analyses that depend on initial cell-type assignments may discard quantitative marker information and inherit annotation errors. Pairwise or composition-based methods may miss multivariate or nonlinear relationships and can produce redundant neighborhoods that require manual consolidation. Supervised graph models may require many labeled samples and often yield representations that are difficult to explain. Global summaries can obscure heterogeneity by treating relationships as uniform across a specimen.

A cell's position within its microenvironment influences its state, function, and interactions with neighboring cells. Spatial domains are therefore characterized jointly by cellular composition and transcriptomic profiles, and resolving those domains is important for studying tissue development, homeostasis, and disease. Current technologies face a trade-off between molecular coverage and spatial resolution. Sequencing-based platforms measure transcriptome-wide expression but collect it in capture regions that may contain several cells, and fixed grids leave parts of a tissue section unmeasured. Imaging-based platforms localize transcripts at single-cell resolution but generally assay a selected panel.

Many computational approaches combine sequencing-based spatial data with a single-cell reference to estimate the composition of each capture region. Composition alone does not provide a transcriptome-wide expression profile for every individual cell, and existing approaches struggle to preserve spatially varying expression when distributing spot-level counts among cells. Information outside capture regions remains unavailable even after within-spot deconvolution. A complete cell-resolved tissue representation would need to reconcile spot counts, individual-cell locations, reference cell states, and spatial variation, while remaining testable against higher-resolution measurements.

Spatially resolved transcriptomics preserves the locations of RNA molecules within tissue and makes it possible to study cellular architecture in situ. Although a tissue section has physical depth, most analyses represent it as a flat two-dimensional plane. Typical sections are several micrometres thick, so a planar projection may combine transcripts that originated from structures located above or below one another.

This projection can create vertical spatial doublets: a segmented object may contain RNA from more than one cell type because distinct cells overlap along the depth axis. Similar mixtures may arise from genuine cellular associations or technical artifacts such as folds. These effects can contaminate cell-type profiles, obscure rare or interspersed populations, and complicate downstream spatial analyses. Their severity may depend on tissue density, cellular morphology, section thickness, and the organization of particular cell types. Sequencing-based assays usually record expression in two dimensions and cannot directly resolve this ambiguity. Imaging-based assays can retain a depth coordinate for individual transcripts even when segmentation and interpretation are subsequently performed in two dimensions. Depth information creates an opportunity to test whether molecular signals assigned to the same planar location remain consistent through a section.

Multicellular tissues depend on coordinated signaling among neighboring cells to maintain homeostasis, organize development, and respond to injury or disease. A common strategy connects ligands produced by sender cells with receptors on receiver cells and downstream transcriptional responses. Single-cell sequencing enables systematic inference of such relationships, but dissociation removes physical arrangement and cannot distinguish interactions that are merely molecularly plausible from those that are spatially feasible.

Spatial transcriptomics preserves tissue location while measuring expression, creating an opportunity to examine communication within local neighborhoods. Platforms vary substantially: some measure mixtures of several cell types per spot, whereas others approach single-cell resolution but assay a restricted panel. Low-resolution spots obscure which cell type produced a ligand and which population expressed a responsive target. Even at higher resolution, sparsity and incomplete coverage complicate inference. Reliable analysis must account for proximity, cell-type composition, receptor availability, and downstream target-gene regulation rather than treating ligand or receptor expression alone as evidence of active signaling. Existing approaches largely emphasize ligand-receptor coexpression and may provide global summaries or scores for individual pairs, but do not directly quantify where a ligand is associated with a coordinated downstream response in a receiver population.

Spatial transcriptomic technologies measure gene expression while retaining tissue coordinates. The landscape includes sequencing-based platforms with broad transcriptome coverage and imaging-based platforms with high spatial or single-cell resolution but more limited gene panels. Studies increasingly collect multiple sections from different donors, orientations, conditions, developmental stages, or technologies. Joint analysis can reveal structures shared across sections and features unique to particular samples, but technical differences and unwanted variation can obscure those relationships.

Many integration methods summarize each cell or spot in a low-dimensional representation and align datasets in that space. For spatial data, successful integration must preserve local neighborhoods and continuous anatomy, not only expression similarity. It must also avoid forcing sample-specific structures to match when they represent genuine biology. These requirements become harder when sections overlap only partially, platform resolution and gene coverage differ, or morphology changes over time. Matrix factorization offers an interpretable alternative by decomposing expression into spatial factors and gene programs, but existing factorization methods often lack mechanisms for complex cross-dataset variation, while integration procedures may not recover interpretable factors.

Spatial transcriptomic assays measure gene expression while retaining the physical locations of cells or capture sites in intact tissue. Tissue organization is not limited to one characteristic scale: a broad anatomical compartment can contain smaller functional regions, and multiple spatial programs may overlap rather than partition a section into mutually exclusive domains. Conventional clustering and segmentation usually assign every observation to one region at a selected resolution. Such partitions can recover dominant anatomy but may miss small structures, divide coherent large regions, or conceal region-within-region organization. The relevant spatial scale can also vary across a single specimen and may not be known in advance.

Coordinated gene expression can be confined to part of an anatomical region, repeated in distant locations, or layered with other programs in the same cells. These patterns are difficult to summarize with one exhaustive partition. Spatial information is also important for interpreting molecular signaling because ligand and receptor expression alone does not establish where communication is physically plausible, and activity can vary among cells with the same annotation. Imaging-based assays may additionally retain depth across serial planes, whereas a two-dimensional summary can discard relationships between layers. Representations of tissue structure therefore need to accommodate localized, overlapping programs and preserve the available geometry without assuming that one fixed scale or grouping explains all spatial variation.

Development, regeneration, and disease progression involve coordinated changes in cell state together with reorganization of tissue. Spatial transcriptomics collected at several time points can observe these processes while preserving the local environments in which cells differentiate. Trajectory-inference methods commonly order cells along pseudotime, estimate transitions between measured populations, or learn a continuous velocity in gene-expression space. These approaches can identify likely ancestors and descendants, but many were designed for dissociated single-cell measurements and either ignore tissue position or connect only adjacent observed time points. A model that predicts later cell states can provide a stronger test of whether the inferred dynamics generalize beyond the observations used for training.

Incorporating space into temporal inference is difficult because sections from different stages are not registered and developing organs can rotate, translate, grow, or change shape. Raw coordinates therefore cannot be compared as if every slice shared one fixed reference frame. Nevertheless, spatial organization contains information about plausible cell fates: transcriptionally similar cells in different anatomical locations may follow different paths, and future populations should appear in biologically coherent regions. Temporal models must combine expression and tissue geometry without confusing tissue movement or shape change with molecular state transitions, while remaining able to extrapolate beyond the measured stages.

Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA in intact tissue and is often interpreted with a single-cell or single-nucleus reference. Deconvolution models use reference profiles to estimate which cell types contribute to each spatial location, while segmentation-based workflows assign molecules to detected cell bodies. Both strategies assume that the relevant expression is represented by the reference or by segmented cells. Tissue dissociation can underrepresent fragile or lipid-rich cell types, and single-nucleus measurements omit much cytoplasmic RNA. Transcripts in axons, dendrites, extracellular regions, or poorly segmented structures can likewise remain outside the units used for conventional analysis.

Unrepresented expression creates two related problems. It can be forced onto similar reference cell types and bias estimated composition, and it can hide spatially organized biology that exists outside canonical cell-body profiles. The overlooked component may contain missing cell types, subcellular programs, or extracellular signals rather than undifferentiated technical noise. Separating reference-explainable expression from the remainder could improve composition estimates and make previously inaccessible spatial signal available for unbiased characterization. Such a separation must work across assay resolutions and reference modalities and distinguish meaningful tissue organization from measurement noise without assuming in advance which biological source was omitted.

Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while retaining the positions of capture spots or cells in intact tissue. This joint view can reveal anatomical organization, local cell states, and interactions that disappear after dissociation. In practice, most sequencing-based spots contain several cells, while imaging-based assays trade broad transcriptome coverage for higher spatial resolution. Experiments may also include serial sections, multiple organs, or different platforms, creating technical and biological differences that must be handled without erasing tissue structure. A useful analysis therefore needs to represent expression and geometry together, rather than treating coordinates as metadata added after ordinary clustering.

Several downstream questions recur across tissues. Analysts want to identify contiguous spatial domains, align sections collected from related specimens, and estimate which cell types contribute to mixed locations. Gene-only clustering can split coherent regions or connect distant areas, and generic batch correction may remove real differences between slices. Reference-based deconvolution can estimate composition but often ignores the neighborhood relationships that make a cell state spatially plausible. The challenge is to learn representations that preserve local continuity, support joint analysis across sections, and transfer single-cell information into spatial measurements while remaining interpretable in histological and biological terms.

Spatially resolved transcriptomics records molecular profiles together with the locations where transcripts were measured. These data make it possible to study tissue architecture at scales ranging from multicellular capture spots to nearly cellular beads or imaging pixels. A tissue section often contains sharp boundaries, gradual transitions, and regions with different cell mixtures, so an analysis must use spatial relationships without assuming that nearby observations are identical. Resolution, sequencing depth, and platform chemistry also vary across experiments, which complicates comparisons among sections and datasets.

A central task is to divide a tissue into biologically meaningful regions while retaining expression patterns near their boundaries. Standard dimensionality reduction and clustering can produce fragmented domains, particularly when neighboring spots contain different cell types or when measurements are sparse. Smoothing can improve continuity but may blur boundaries and create artificial expression. Spatial data can also be collected as consecutive sections, allowing three-dimensional reconstruction and requiring correction of section-specific effects. Methods that learn a low-dimensional representation from expression and local neighborhoods should therefore be assessed for domain accuracy, denoising behavior, cross-section integration, and their ability to recover coherent three-dimensional organization.

Cells in a tissue are embedded in local microenvironments whose composition, organization, and molecular activity can differ across a section. Spatial omics makes it possible to describe these environments while preserving coordinates, but the measurements are often sparse and collected at different resolutions. A neighborhood may contain several cell types, and the same cell type can participate in distinct environments. Summaries based only on global expression or isolated cell labels can therefore miss local heterogeneity, especially at disease boundaries or in tissues with complex architecture.

Analyses of spatial heterogeneity need to compare neighborhoods rather than only individual spots. They may quantify how similar two local compositions are, identify recurrent microenvironments, detect regions that differ between conditions, and connect spatial patterns with ligand–receptor activity or tissue annotations. Reliable comparisons must account for unequal neighborhood sizes, continuous transitions, and multiple spatial dimensions. They should also distinguish a real change in local organization from a change caused by cell density or platform resolution. A useful framework consequently combines spatial geometry with cell-state composition and provides interpretable scores for heterogeneity, differential neighborhoods, and putative interactions.

Spatial transcriptomics can measure thousands of genes while preserving where each spot or cell lies in a tissue. This makes it possible to ask not only which cell states are present, but also how they are arranged and how those arrangements change during development, injury, or disease. Spatial measurements can be obtained from capture arrays, beads, or imaging assays, and may range from multicellular spots to subcellular locations. The resulting datasets contain both molecular variation and geometric structure, with sparsity and uneven sampling complicating direct comparisons.

Many biological processes unfold as transitions between states that occupy related positions in a tissue. Ordinary pseudotime methods often use expression similarity alone, connect cells that are far apart, or compare time points without accounting for tissue growth and rearrangement. A spatially aware analysis should learn a representation that respects local neighborhoods, delineate domains, and provide a continuous ordering of locations when a process is likely to progress through space. It should also support expression-pattern discovery and communication analysis, so that inferred trajectories can be tested against anatomy, marker genes, and known cell–cell relationships.

Sequencing-based spatial transcriptomics provides broad gene coverage but measures RNA in capture regions that can contain several adjacent cells. The resulting profile is a mixture whose apparent marker genes may reflect neighboring tissue rather than the cell type assigned to a spot. Misassigned or swapped spots can blur anatomical boundaries, reduce marker specificity, and distort downstream clustering or estimates of malignant composition. The problem is especially important when tissue regions have similar expression programs or when a small amount of contamination crosses a sharp interface.

A correction strategy must detect suspicious locations using both expression and tissue geometry, then replace or repair them without inventing patterns that are not supported by nearby observations. It should be testable on mixtures with known species labels or on tissues with gold-standard annotations and should improve the specificity of marker genes, domains, and cell-type calls. Performance may depend on how many spots are affected, whether the contamination is local or distant, and whether the tissue contains multiple biological boundaries. Spatial quality control is therefore a prerequisite for interpreting many downstream analyses rather than a cosmetic preprocessing step.

Spatial molecular assays combine high-dimensional measurements with a coordinate system and, in many experiments, a matched microscopy image. The observations may be spots, cells, nuclei, pixels, or subcellular locations, and the neighborhood relation appropriate for one technology may be inappropriate for another. Modern studies also generate images that are too large to load into memory at once. Analysis software must therefore represent spatial graphs and image data efficiently while keeping molecular and morphological observations linked.

Common questions include whether cell types are spatially enriched near one another, which genes show spatially patterned expression, how tissue regions are organized, and whether morphology agrees with molecular structure. These tasks require flexible definitions of neighbors, statistics for local and global patterning, and image operations such as tiling, segmentation, and feature extraction. A reusable toolkit should support multiple assay types, scale to large images and datasets, expose interpretable outputs, and interoperate with established single-cell data structures so that spatial analyses can be composed into reproducible workflows.

Spatial transcriptomics offers a compromise between transcriptome-wide sequencing and preservation of tissue context. Each measured location has a molecular profile and coordinates, yet the signal can be sparse, noisy, and collected at very different resolutions. A useful representation should retain biological variation while encoding which locations are neighbors. Such representations can support domain detection, visualization, trajectory inference, batch correction, denoising, and recovery of expression that is obscured by dropout.

Many existing embeddings are learned from expression alone or add coordinates only after dimensionality reduction. Expression-only representations may connect transcriptionally similar but distant regions, whereas overly strong spatial smoothing can merge boundaries and erase rare states. High-resolution assays also produce far more locations than conventional pipelines can process efficiently. The challenge is to learn a compact latent space that combines gene-level structure with a spatial neighborhood graph, remains usable across platforms, and yields quantitative improvements on both annotated tissue organization and noisy expression reconstruction.

Development, injury, and disease alter cell states while reorganizing the tissue around them. Spatial transcriptomics can observe these changes in place, but the data are usually collected from separate sections or time points rather than from one registered three-dimensional specimen. A computational analysis must combine expression, physical distance, and, when available, tissue morphology. It should be able to work with assays that have images as well as assays that provide only coordinates and expression, because spatial studies differ widely in platform and resolution.

Three recurring goals are to trace a biological process through neighboring locations, identify cell–cell communication that is spatially plausible, and reduce noise or missing measurements. Expression or ligand–receptor co-occurrence alone can produce false positives when cells are distant, while morphology-only features cannot identify molecular state. Trajectories may also be distorted by tissue growth or by a mixture of cell types in one spot. Integrative analyses therefore need explicit neighborhood constraints, interpretable contributions from each data modality, and validations using known anatomy, time courses, or independent imaging and expression measurements.

Spatially resolved expression measurements make it possible to study cells and gene programs in the geometry of an intact tissue. Imaging assays can localize many transcripts to individual cells, while capture and bead-based assays provide broader transcriptome coverage at coarser or variable resolution. These technologies reveal tissue organization but also introduce uneven cell density, irregular neighborhoods, and, in some experiments, a third spatial dimension. Statistical methods that ignore density can mistake crowded regions for molecular patterning or miss patterns in sparse regions.

Useful spatial summaries should identify genes whose expression is organized in space, group genes that share a spatial pattern, and test whether complementary signals in neighboring cell types are consistent with communication. The same framework should accommodate two-dimensional sections, aligned serial or volumetric data, and different measurement technologies. It must separate biological spatial heterogeneity from variation caused by density, normalize data appropriately, and provide significance measures that can be checked across animals, layers, or tissue regions. These requirements motivate analyses based on explicit spatial adjacency rather than expression similarity alone.
